Sadie had come for a reason she hadn't fully explained to anyone: two weeks ago her mother had sat at the kitchen counter with a lease renewal letter and said, mostly to herself, that twelve years of rent had bought them exactly nothing. Sadie wanted to know if that was true.

Inside, the house smelled like lemon polish and fresh paint, which was the smell of somebody trying. Mr. Wardak, the owner, stood by the fireplace shaking hands. He was their neighbor from four doors down, the one who had eulogized his own hedge for an entire block party after the city made him cut it back, and he greeted Sadie by name. "You brought your checkbook?" he said. "Sixteen, seventeen-year-old, you could be my competition." He said it warmly, but Sadie noticed how his eyes moved to the signup sheet, tallying who might actually bid.

Addyson drifted toward the kitchen while Bastien, who had tagged along because his shift at the pharmacy didn't start until three, planted himself in the living room with his phone. "This house is listed at three ninety," he said. "I'm running it." He typed, frowned, tilted the screen away from a passing stranger. "Okay, wait. If you borrow three hundred thousand for thirty years at six percent fixed, the interest alone is more than three forty-seven. That's more than you borrowed. You pay for the house twice and then some." Sadie took the phone. The number sat on the screen, patient and recalcitrant, refusing to become smaller the longer she stared.

"That can't be right," she said. Bastien shrugged and re-ran it. Same total. A couple near the window was murmuring about whether they'd need to put twenty percent down, and Sadie asked them, before she could decide not to, what happened if you didn't. The man said you paid extra every month, insurance for the lender, and the woman added that they'd saved nine years for their down payment and were still short. Nine years. Sadie's mother had been saving, in theory, since Sadie was nine.

Mr. Wardak found her by the staircase. "You look like somebody handed you a bill," he said, and she told him the interest number, watching to see whether he'd flinch. He didn't. He said the house had been in his family thirty-one years, that his father had signed the papers at a kitchen table like this one, that when his father died the mortgage outlived him for six more years. "The bank got its money either way," he said. "But my mother paid it off the last winter she was alive, and she sat in that chair," pointing at the window seat, "like a queen." Sadie asked if he was selling because he had to. He straightened a curtain that didn't need straightening. "Because it's time," he said, which answered nothing.

In the kitchen, the woman from the couple was explaining earnest money to Addyson: you hand over a deposit when you make an offer, a few thousand, to show you're serious, and it goes toward the purchase if the deal closes. Addyson said that sounded like betting on a house, and the woman laughed and said it was worse than betting because at least a bet ends quickly. Sadie thought of the interest number again, then of her mother's lease letter, twelve years of payments that had ended every month, cleanly, like a door closing. There was something almost merciful in it. There was also something in Mr. Wardak's mother sitting in that window seat.

She found Bastien on the porch steps and sat down beside him. "Say somebody could rent forever and never own anything," she said, "or borrow and end up paying more than the house is worth before it's hers. Which one loses less?" Bastien said it depended on how long you lived there, whether the value went up, what else you did with the money, and then admitted he was repeating things his sister said about her student loans. "So nobody knows," Sadie said. "Nobody knows," Bastien agreed, and ate the cookie Addyson had abandoned on the railing.

Before leaving, Sadie went back inside to tell Mr. Wardak something, though she hadn't decided what. He was standing at the window seat, and when he turned she only said, "How much was the deposit?" He smiled like she'd asked the right question at last. "In this state, on a house like this, maybe five thousand," he said. "In 1973, my father put down eight hundred dollars and a handshake." Behind him, on the signup sheet, a twelfth name appeared in fresh ink. Sadie looked at it, then out the window at her own street, four doors down, where the porch light her mother never remembered to turn off was burning in the middle of the day.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Many driving courses teach keeping at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and a longer gap in rain, snow or darkness.
story:
Ms. Vu's Buick smelled like cough drops and old radio, and Brooklyn had the keys to it because Ms. Vu had cataract surgery on Tuesday and a craving for canned pears on Wednesday. "You drive," Ms. Vu had said from her porch, holding a shopping list folded into a square the size of a stamp. "I supervise. I'm told supervising is all the rage."

That was how Brooklyn ended up in the grocery store parking lot at four in the afternoon, the test eight days away, easing the Buick between a minivan and a hydrant with Ms. Vu narrating from the passenger seat like a golf announcer. "You have room," she murmured. "You have less room. You have no room at all." Brooklyn cut the wheel, straightened, and looked in the mirror. Eight inches from the curb. Nine, if she was being generous to herself, which after four attempts she had earned.

"You're improving," Ms. Vu said. "My nephew failed that part twice. He blamed the cones, the weather, and the province." Brooklyn laughed, and then didn't, because the truth was that the parking wasn't what kept her up at night. The parking was a matter of geometry. The highway merge was a matter of nerve.

Her father had opinions about nerve. He believed that merging was a contest you won by committing fully, signals be damned, hesitation being the thing that actually got people killed. Ms. Vu believed, apparently, that the road was a cooperative enterprise and that space was a form of kindness. Brooklyn had spent two weeks trying to figure out which of them to believe, and had mostly concluded that both were terrifying in a rental car.

Inside the store she pushed the cart while Ms. Vu supervised the pears. Frederik appeared at the end of the canned goods aisle like a prophecy, in his green apron, restocking chickpeas. "You passed?" he asked, before hello.

"Test's next week. I'm chauffeuring."

"Chauffeuring," Frederik repeated, and leaned on the shelf. He had a plan, and Brooklyn knew its shape before he said it, because Frederik's plans all had the same shape. "The show is the fifteenth. Yousif's sister will drive us there but nobody will drive us back, because she's staying for the late set, and the bus after eleven is a rumor." He picked up a can of chickpeas and looked at it as if it might endorse him. "So really this is about the arts."

"It's about you not wanting to ride the rumor bus."

"That is the arts," Frederik said, and went back to his shelf, radiating the patience of someone who believed the matter settled.

In the car on the way home, Ms. Vu directed her onto the ring road, "for practice," and Brooklyn's hands went cold on the wheel before she'd even found the ramp. The traffic was thick but moving, and there was a transport truck two lanes over that seemed to be in every mirror at once. She checked her mirror, her blind spot, her mirror again, and then, instead of lungging in, she held back behind a silver hatchback and did the thing the driving book had taught her, the thing she'd practiced aloud on her bedroom ceiling. The hatchback passed a green exit sign, and she said nothing, and the sign slid past her own window a moment later. "One," she said, out loud, before she could stop herself.

"One what?" Ms. Vu asked.

"One second. You're supposed to have at least a two-second gap behind the car ahead." She watched the next sign go by. "Two. Okay." The road was dry and bright, so two was what the book asked for; she remembered the page saying to stretch it out in rain or snow or darkness, which had seemed fussy until she pictured doing any of this at night in the rain. In front of her the hatchback's driver had already begun to close the gap, drifting up on a minivan, and Brooklyn eased off the gas to keep her own margin, and the merge lane arrived, and she slid into the space she'd saved like it had been reserved.

"Well," Ms. Vu said. "That was almost boring."

"Thank you," Brooklyn said, and meant it as the highest available praise.

She thought about it at the next red light, hands at ten and two. Her father would have called her gap cowardice, an invitation for the whole world to cut in, and on the way home one car did cut in, and she counted again, one, two, and let it. Maybe commitment and space weren't actually opposites; maybe the merge wanted both at once, decisiveness about where you were going and stubborn generosity about the distance you kept, and maybe that combination was something you had to remake every thirty seconds rather than decide once. She couldn't have written it as a rule. It felt more like a thing she'd have to keep doing until it was hers, or until it wasn't.

Ms. Vu directed her off at the exit with the drugstore, then back toward the parking lot, and had her parallel park one more time between two carts somebody had abandoned. Six inches from the curb. Inside the store, visible through the glass, Frederik was at the register now, ringing up a woman's groceries with unusual grace, the way he did when he wanted the world to notice he existed. He caught Brooklyn's eye through the window and held up one finger, tilted his head toward a wall calendar by the lottery tickets, the fifteenth circled twice in green pen.

She still had the test. She still had a father with opinions and a Thursday night highway run scheduled with him, in his car, his way. She held up one finger back at Frederik, meaning maybe, meaning ask me after, meaning she genuinely did not know yet, and put the Buick in park.

"Am I allowed to say the pears were worth it?" Ms. Vu asked, gathering her bags.

"Say whatever you want," Brooklyn said. "I'm counting to two first."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Canada's 2019 food guide suggests filling half the plate with vegetables and fruits, a quarter with protein foods and a quarter with whole grain foods.
story:
Dominic counted the onions twice before he put them in the cart, because onions were the only thing on the list he was sure about. The community kitchen on Hale Street ran a six-week course called Cooking for One, and Mr. Nur, who ran it, had sent them off with a single instruction: plan seven dinners, buy everything, cook what you can in one afternoon. The other four in the course were older, retired mostly, except Raine, who was taking a gap year and had argued with the self-checkout machine for five minutes before the cashier came over.

"Half the plate," Raine said, holding up the folded handout from week one. They were standing in the produce section, and the fluorescent light made every pepper look lit from inside. "Half the plate vegetables and fruits. A quarter protein foods, a quarter whole grain foods. That's what it says. Canada's food guide, 2019. I kept the page." Dominic took the paper and looked at it, then looked at his list, which read, in full: pasta, sauce, chicken, maybe eggs? He had written the question mark himself.

The problem was not ambition. The problem was that Dominic had never thought of a plate as something with proportions. At home his mother cooked, and when she worked nights he ate cereal standing at the counter, and neither of those had ever seemed like decisions. Now the handout turned every dinner into a small geometry problem, and he stood in the aisle trying to imagine a plate divided, and failed, and felt the pugnacious part of himself rise up and say that a person could eat whatever he wanted. Then a second voice, quieter, said that the whole reason he'd signed up was that he was leaving for residence in September and did not want to live on whatever the nearest vending machine offered.

So he rebuilt the list right there, leaning on the cart. If half the plate was vegetables and fruits, then he needed more of those than anything else: peppers, a bag of carrots, two cans of tomatoes, a bag of frozen peas because Raine swore by frozen. A quarter protein foods meant some chicken, a dozen eggs, one can of beans. A quarter whole grain foods meant brown rice and a kind of pasta that cost a dollar more than the kind he liked. He did the math in his head, roughly, and it came to less than he'd feared. The guide wasn't a rule, he decided; it was a way of turning the huge blank question of feeding yourself into something with edges.

Back at the kitchen, Mr. Nur had the ovens preheated and six cutting boards laid out like exam desks. He moved through the room without lecturing, which Dominic appreciated, pausing only to correct knife grips and to lift the lid on a pot at exactly the right moment. When Dominic confessed he'd rebuilt his list in the supermarket aisle, Mr. Nur said only, "Good. That's where the real class happens." Raine, at the next station, burned the first tray of roasted vegetables and stood looking at it with an expression of genuine philosophical injury, as though the universe had betrayed a contract.

From Raine's side of the room, the afternoon looked different than Dominic knew it did. She watched him brown chicken in batches, wipe down the board between each batch, write times and temperatures in the margin of his handout with the concentration of someone defusing something. She had thought he was the confident kind, the kind who signed up for things and then coasted. But his hands shook slightly when he carried the sheet pan, and he apologized to the oven, out loud, when he opened it too early and let the heat out. She decided she liked him better with heat escaping.

The crisis came at four o'clock, when Dominic realized that seven dinners cooked in one afternoon meant seven containers cooling on one inadequate rack, and that he had not thought about the middle of the week, when the food would be four days old and he would be tired and the whole tidy plan would slide back toward entropy, toward cereal, toward nothing. He stood in front of the containers with his list in his hand and no idea what to do.

Mr. Nur slid a stack of containers across the counter toward him, the kind that went from freezer to oven. "Freeze half of Thursday and Friday," he said. "Thaw Wednesday night." It was so obvious that Dominic laughed, a short embarrassed sound, and Raine laughed too, and then helped him label the lids in her slanted handwriting. The frozen containers went into the big freezer down the hall, a small ordered column on an empty shelf.

Walking home, Dominic carried the bag against his hip, cold leaking through the canvas, and he thought about his mother's kitchen and about the plate divided in half and quarters, and about how he still didn't know whether he'd actually eat the peas or whether they'd sit in the freezer like a promise he'd made to a version of himself he hadn't met yet. He took out his phone and texted Raine: same time next week? The streetlights came on as he waited at the corner, and the bag sweated against his jeans.

"Bring your own container," Raine texted back. "Mr. Nur says next week is soup."

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: In the United States, every new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9, which verifies identity and permission to work, no later than their first day of paid work.
story:
The marquee of the Odeon still said SUMMER CLASSICS in letters that had faded to the color of weak tea, and Coralie stood under it for a full minute before she went in, telling herself that the interview had already happened, that the hard part was over, and that today was only orientation. Inside, the lobby smelled of melted butter and floor cleaner, and a woman in a navy vest was waiting for her beside the popcorn machine with a clipboard and a pen on a string.

"You must be Coralie," the woman said. "I'm Ms. Friedman. You'll start on registers tonight if the paperwork goes through."

She said it lightly, the way people say things they assume will go smoothly, and handed over the clipboard. The top page was a form Coralie had never seen before, dense with small print, a header that read Employment Eligibility Verification, and a first section marked SECTION 1, EMPLOYEE INFORMATION AND ATTESTATION. Below that, a warning in bold: this section had to be completed no later than the first day of paid work. She read it twice, because the phrase seemed to be addressed directly to her, and she was, as of this morning, someone with a first day of paid work.

The trouble arrived quietly. She filled in her name, her address, the date. Then the form asked her to attest that she was a citizen, a national, a lawful permanent resident, or something else, and to check a box. She checked the first one without hesitation. But beneath the attestation, in even smaller print, it said that a parent or guardian had to sign if the employee was younger than eighteen, and her mother was forty minutes away at the clinic where she worked, and the shift began at five.

"Can I take it home and bring it back tomorrow?" Coralie asked.

Ms. Friedman's face did something careful. "The rule is it has to be done no later than your first day of paid work," she said. "Today is your first day."

"Then I'm not paid yet," Coralie said. "I haven't done anything."

"You're on the schedule at five."

The logic of it sat between them like a coin neither would pick up. Coralie thought of her civics class, where Ms. Friedman's counterpart at school, a man who treated every rule as a load-bearing wall, had once said that a polity runs on forms as much as on laws, that the paperwork is where the promise becomes enforceable. She had found that parochial at the time, too narrow a view of what held a country together, and she had said so, arguing that trust underwrote institutions more than documents did. Now she stood inside one of those institutions, holding a document, and the argument collapsed into something practical: her mother's signature, or no shift.

She called her mother, who did not answer, which was normal. She called again. Kristian, who worked weekends at the ticket booth and had gotten her the interview in the first place, leaned out of the booth window.

"Everything okay?"

"There's a form," Coralie said. "It verifies I'm allowed to work. I have to finish the first part today, no later than my first day, and my mom has to sign it because I'm under eighteen, and she's at work."

Kristian came out, wiping his hands on his trousers. "Mine signed it in the car," he said. "My dad drove me. Do you have anybody closer?"

There was her neighbor, Allan, a retired postman who was, technically, not her guardian but who had driven her to the dentist twice when her mother's shifts made it impossible. She did not know if a neighbor could sign. She suspected not. She also suspected that the honest answer was to ask, rather than to guess, and that guessing wrong would be worse than the small humiliation of asking.

"Ms. Friedman," she said, "does it have to be my mom, or any parent or guardian?"

"Parent or guardian," Ms. Friedman said, and added, almost kindly, "You could come back for tomorrow's shift."

Coralie looked at the schedule taped behind the counter, where her name was written in the five o'clock row in blue pen, and she thought about the difference between the rule as an obstacle and the rule as a floor, something to stand on rather than something blocked by. The form was not trying to keep her out. It was the mechanism by which she was let in, the proof that the Odeon had checked, that she had attested, that everything was aboveboard. It was inconvenient in exactly the way that honest things are often inconvenient.

"My mom's off at four thirty," she said. "If I go now, she can sign it and I can be back by five. Is that allowed?"

Ms. Friedman considered. "Section 1 completed no later than your first day of paid work," she said, reading the bold line back to her. "Paid work. If the paperwork is in my hand before you clock in, you're fine. You'd be riding a bike forty minutes."

"It's mostly downhill coming back."

Kristian unlocked his own bike from the rack by the doors. "Take mine," he said. "It's faster and I don't clock in until Saturday."

She pedaled up Elm with the form folded in her back pocket, the paper crinkling against her with every stroke, her mother's clinic three streets past the top of the hill. She would explain it badly and her mother would understand anyway, the way she always did, and the signature would take ten seconds, and the ride home would be fast with the sun behind her.

At the clinic door she pulled the form out, smoothed it flat against the glass, and went in.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Because several codons can code for the same amino acid, some single-base mutations change nothing in the finished protein; these are called silent mutations.
story:
Justin had agreed to spend his Thursday evening at the community garden before he remembered the genetics quiz, and by the time he remembered, it was too late to back out without lying. The quiz was at eight the next morning. It covered transcription and translation, which Mr. Fitzgerald had described as the single most important idea of the semester, and which Justin could recite on paper but could not, so far, actually explain to anyone.

The garden sat behind the recycling depot, twenty plots behind a chain-link fence, and it belonged in the evenings to Mr. Marino, a retired plumber who ran the youth plots and kept a thermos of coffee that smelled like burnt toast. Carissa was already there when Justin arrived, kneeling in the herb bed with her textbook wedged open against a stake, a trowel in one hand. She had the same quiz. She had also, apparently, decided that both things could happen at once.

"You're late," she said, without looking up. "Mr. Marino already yelled at the pigeons twice."

"There was a bus," Justin said, which was true enough, and he pulled on the gloves hanging from the fence and knelt beside her in the onion rows. The work was weeding, steady and simple, and Mr. Marino had promised them each a bag of tomatoes if they finished the row before dark. That was the deal. Dark came at nine. It was already seven.

He remembered Tuesday in class, the way you remember a small accident. Mr. Fitzgerald had put a strand of DNA on the board, a short stretch of letters, and had them copy it down. Then he had changed one letter, a single base, and asked what would happen to the protein. Justin had written "the amino acid changes," because that was the pattern, the thing you were supposed to see. The kid beside him had written the same. When Mr. Fitzgerald revealed that in this particular example nothing in the finished protein changed at all, that the protein came out identical, half the room had made that low noise a class makes when it suspects a trick.

"That's the part I don't get," Justin said now, working his trowel under a clump of crabgrass. "Tuesday. He changed a letter and then said the protein was the same. That breaks the whole system. One letter, one amino acid. That's how it works. That's the only thing I actually understand."

Carissa sat back on her heels. "Maybe it doesn't break it. Maybe it's the system." She flipped the textbook around in the dirt so he could see, and there it was again, the codon chart, the grid he'd been avoiding all week. He had treated that chart like something to memorize the night before, an enemy to be defeated by flashlight under the covers. She was treating it like a map.

He wiped his gloves on his knees and took the book. Transcription first: the DNA letters get copied into a message. Then translation: the message gets read in groups of three, each group an amino acid, the amino acids chained into a protein. Fine. He traced the example with his finger, the original and the changed version side by side. Same message length. Same reading. The changed letter fell inside one of the groups of three, and when he ran his finger down the chart, the changed group still pointed to the exact same amino acid. Not a different one. The same one. The chart was redundant, the same amino acid sitting in more than one cell, so a changed letter could land you right back where you started.

"Wait," he said. "Wait, wait. Several of these codons mean the same amino acid. So a one-letter change can give you a different codon that still codes for the same amino acid. The protein comes out identical. Nothing changes in the finished protein. It's like writing 'colour' with a u or without, it's still the same word." He said it out loud and felt something in his chest go quiet, as though the confusion had been a bleeding thing and naming it had cauterized it.

"Silent mutations," Carissa said. "That's what they're called. It's on page two-twelve, I read it last night." She took the book back with the mild authority of someone who had done the reading and was not going to be dramatic about it.

Aicha arrived then, bike helmet still buckled, because she had missed the whole week with the flu and had the quiz on Friday, one day after theirs. She had heard about the garden through the group chat, which in the last week of the semester had taken on a zeitgeist of pure panic, every message a photograph of someone's notes at one in the morning. She knelt in the dirt between them and said, "Tell me everything. Explain it like I'm a plant."

So Justin explained it, haltingly, using the onions. "This row is the DNA. Okay? It doesn't move. It stays here." He pinched a weed, pulled it, laid it in the path. "But the cell needs the instructions out where the work happens, so it copies the row." He laid a second line of weeds beside the first, shorter, crooked. "That's transcription. The copy gets carried out and read in threes, and every three makes one piece, and the pieces get chained together. That's the protein. That's translation." He heard himself saying it and realized it was the first time the whole thing had come out of him in order, out loud, in a sentence another person could follow.

"Does every mistake ruin the protein?" Aicha asked.

"No," Justin said, and he told her about Tuesday, the changed letter, the protein that came out exactly the same, several codons pointing at the same amino acid. He told her the name Carissa had given him. He did not pretend, even to her, that he understood why the code was built that way, why the redundancy existed at all; that was a question he was willing to leave open, and he said so, and Aicha nodded as though an honest gap was more useful to her than a false floor.

The light was thinning over the recycling depot, and Mr. Marino came down the row with the hose, checking their work, saying nothing, which was his version of approval. Carissa closed the textbook and pressed the dirt flat around the onions. Justin looked at the row, at the copy he had made of it in weeds, and got up to fetch the stake and string for the tomatoes before the dark came and the deal expired. "Same time Sunday," Aicha called after him. "Bring the chart."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.
story:
The elevator in the Harrow Court building smelled like cardboard and lemon cleaner, and Levi rode it eleven floors with a box of records balanced against his hip, watching the numbers change. Three days ago he had lived forty minutes from Malika and Ilias, close enough that a bike ride could settle an argument. Now the hallway carpet was a color he had no name for, somewhere between rust and regret, and the apartment behind him held his mother's half-unpacked pans and his father's voice on the phone saying the transfer was good for the family, all things considered.

He had promised himself he would not mope. Moping, according to Ilias, was a lifestyle choice, and Ilias had eviscerated him for it once, in the laconic way he had, one sentence that left nothing standing: "You're allowed to be sad, but you're not allowed to be boring about it." Levi had laughed then, in the parking lot after their last exam. He had not laughed much since, though he kept trying the sentence on in the new rooms, testing whether it still fit.

On the fourth evening, Mr. Mori from 11B knocked on their door with a plate of gyoza and an apology for the smell of frying that had drifted down the hall. He was retired, he said, widowed, and he watched the news at six whether or not anything was happening. Levi stood in the doorway holding the plate while the television behind Mr. Mori's shoulder kept murmuring, and a phrase surfaced out of it, read in the anchor's flat cadence. The Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, had issued an advisory in May 2023, and it described loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.

"An epidemic," Mr. Mori said, mostly to himself, spooning dipping sauce into a smaller container. "Like something you could catch." He handed the sauce over and asked whether Levi's family had found the good grocery store yet, and Levi said they had found a store, and the door closed, and he stood in the rust-colored hallway holding warm food and thinking: an epidemic. He had assumed loneliness was private, a personal failure of nerve. The word advisory suggested it was also official, a thing measured at the level of a country. Both of those could be true at once, he supposed, though he was not sure yet how they fit together.

He took the gyoza to his room and set it on the desk beside the shoebox of things he had refused to pack properly: a broken headphone, a ticket stub, the group photo from junior year where Malika had blinked. His phone sat face-down where he had left it that morning. He and Malika and Ilias had said they would text, and they did text, but the texts had the stiffness of letters, each one composed rather than spoken. He wondered whether distance did that on its own, or whether you had to let it. He wondered, too, whether calling would feel desperate, and then wondered who had taught him to use that word for wanting to talk to his friends.

In the morning he carried the empty plate down to 11B, mostly as an excuse. Mr. Mori was repotting a ficus on newspaper spread across his kitchen floor, and he invited Levi in without looking up. The apartment was small and exact, every object in its decided place. Levi asked whether the news last night had said anything more about the advisory, and Mr. Mori said it had not, that the news moved on, that he remembered a time when neighbors borrowed ladders from each other. "Not nostalgia," he said, tapping soil from the old pot. "Observation."

"Then it's catchable in both directions," Levi said. "If isolation spreads, company probably does too." He had not planned to say it out loud, and once he had, it sounded like something Ilias would test with a skeptical eyebrow. Mr. Mori considered it while he settled the ficus into fresh soil. "That's a nice theory," he said. "You could be an apologist for almost anything with a theory like that." But he was smiling a little, and he told Levi that the building had a rooftop with chairs nobody used, and that a person could sit up there with a phone signal strong enough for anything.

That evening Levi climbed to the roof with the last of the gyoza gone cold in his pocket and watched the unfamiliar skyline organize itself into streetlights. He took out his phone. He thought about the advisory, about May 2023, about an epidemic named by a Surgeon General in a country that included, apparently, one boy on a rooftop. He did not feel cured of anything, and he did not entirely trust the neat symmetry he had proposed to Mr. Mori, the way loneliness and company might balance like weights on a scale. What he knew was smaller and more concrete: that his thumb knew Malika's number, and that the sun was not yet down on the town where she lived.

He pressed call, and while it rang he heard the stairwell door open behind him, and Ilias's laconic voice could not possibly be there, so he did not turn around until a voice did speak, and it was only Mr. Mori with a thermos, saying, "I thought there might be chairs up here worth borrowing." Then the line clicked, and Malika said, "Levi?" and he said, "Hey. I have a whole story for you about the Surgeon General," and he patted the chair beside him.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Anthony had the gym key on a shoelace around his neck, which seemed to him a ridiculous and wonderful thing for a senior to be allowed to wear. Mr. Brown had handed it over in October with the words "They're yours on Tuesdays," and since then the seventh-grade team had scrimmaged every practice, because scrimmaging was easy to run and the boys loved it and loved him for letting them do it. They lost every game by margins that had stopped being embarrassing and become geological.

He was in the library on a Wednesday, supposedly doing a history essay, when Elsa slid into the chair across from him and dropped a photocopy on his textbook. "For your peasants," she said. The article was about musicians, not peasants. He read three paragraphs before he understood she had marked the wrong pages, and then he kept reading anyway, because something in it had already hooked him. Researchers led by a man named Ericsson had studied violinists in 1993 and found that the best ones hadn't just logged the most hours. What separated them was effortful work on specific weaknesses, with immediate feedback. The article called it deliberate practice, and Anthony sat with his chin on his fist and thought about thirty passes a seventh grader could miss without ever being told how.

Kurt found him at lunch and listened to the whole thing while eating fries off Anthony's tray. "So no scrimmage Tuesday," Kurt said.

"Twenty minutes of passing drills. Maybe thirty. Then scrimmage."

"You're going to be less popular."

"I know."

Tuesday came and Anthony set up cones in pairs, three meters apart, and made them pass, and when the ball wobbled he made them do it again. He stood between two boys, Marco and the small one everyone called Mouse, and called every touch: inside foot, eyes up, step to the ball. Marco rolled his eyes so hard that Anthony nearly sent him running laps, which would have been pure Mr. Brown, pure eighth grade, pure everything he had promised himself he wouldn't be. Instead he said, "Again," and Marco passed again, cleaner.

The memory that surfaced was from two years earlier, when Anthony himself had been the one rolling his eyes. His own coach in those days, a man the whole town seemed to lionize, had spent every practice on scrimmages and long speeches about heart, and Anthony had loved him, and had never gotten better at anything except loving him. He had left that program with a weak left foot and a shelf of trophies nobody in the city, that whole cosmopolitan crowd of club coaches and recruiters, had ever cared about. He could admit now that the drills he was running were the drills he'd needed, though he couldn't decide whether that made them right for these boys or only satisfying for him, whether he was coaching them or repairing his own past by proxy.

By the fourth Tuesday there was a shape to it. He had learned to name the specific weakness before he planned anything: their passes died on the ground, so every drill lived on the ground; their heads dropped before release, so he stood behind the receiver and held up fingers, and the passer had to say the number. Mouse, who had been almost a different phylum of player in October, something slow and separate from the rest, now called "Two!" and hit Marco's left foot on the run. Nobody applauded, but Marco didn't have to trap it first, and Anthony felt the change in the way a person feels weather turning.

The day before their last game, Mr. Brown came and stood at the door with his coffee, saying nothing for ten minutes, which was his way of supervising. When Anthony blew the whistle to end a drill and let the scrimmage start, Mr. Brown said, "You've turned them into workers."

"Some of them," Anthony said. "Some of them still just want to play."

"Which are the ones getting better?"

"The ones who hate the drills, mostly." Anthony wiped his hands on his shorts. "I don't know if that means I should make them hate it more or less."

Mr. Brown laughed into his cup and left the doorway, and Anthony understood that he'd been given neither approval nor correction, and would have to decide which it was himself.

They won the last game, four to two, on a goal that began as a one-touch pass from Mouse to Marco's left foot. Elsa had come to watch and sat with Kurt, and afterward she said, "So your peasants liked your violin article," and Kurt said the second goal was offside, loudly, so that half the parents heard him. Anthony gathered the cones while the boys took turns carrying the ball bag like a trophy. He still didn't know whether thirty minutes of repetition was a kindness or a theft of the only years they'd get to just play, and he turned the question over the way he'd turned the gym key in his pocket all season, without once finding a side that felt entirely smooth.

"Same time Tuesday?" Marco called from the door.

"Off season," Anthony said. "But yeah. Same time Tuesday."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Fat bloom is a dull grey or white streaky film that appears on chocolate that was not properly tempered or has melted and reset.
story:
The folding table outside the tent wobbled on its aluminum legs, and Jack steadied it with a flat stone before he set the double boiler down. He had watched four videos on the drive up, and in his notebook he had copied the numbers the way other people copied scripture: melt to forty-five degrees, cool to twenty-seven, bring it back up to thirty-one. Precise. Almost ceremonial. His mother had laughed at the bag of couverture chips riding shotgun the whole six hours, but she had not argued, because Jack had been talking about the farmers market stall since spring, and she knew what it meant to him.

"You're doing the chocolate thing," Barrett said, arriving from the lake with his towel around his neck and lake water still dripping off his forearms. "In a campsite. With a camp stove. You understand that you're insane."

"It's a test run." Jack clipped the thermometer to the saucepan. "If I can do it here, I can do it anywhere. That's the whole point of a test run."

Mr. Tremblay, two sites over, was rinsing a coffee pot at the shared tap, and he wandered over with the unhurried interest of a man with nothing scheduled. "Tempering," he said, reading the notebook upside down. "My sister did that for a living. Twenty years in a patisserie." Jack braced himself for a speech, but the old man only asked whether he could watch, and sat down on the picnic bench like a judge taking his seat for arbitration, saying nothing more, which Jack found both unnerving and oddly respectful. He had expected to be corrected. Instead he was merely observed.

The first batch seized. Jack had known there was a risk of water getting in, but knowing a risk and watching your glossy dark liquid turn into a gritty paste were, he was discovering, two different experiences. He scraped it out, cleaned everything twice, and started over while Barrett narrated like a sports announcer and Kylee, drawn over by the smell, sat cross-legged in the grass fileting the story of her driving test for anyone who would listen, then pausing mid-sentence because Jack had gone completely silent, hovering over the pan like the next thirty seconds were tectonic, capable of reshaping everything.

He cooled the melted chocolate on the marble slab his mother had let him pack, moving it with the spatula in long flat strokes, and when the thermometer touched twenty-seven he moved it back over the gentle heat and brought it up to thirty-one, and the surface held a satin sheen that made Barrett say, quietly, "Okay. That's actually beautiful." Jack dipped a spoon, laid it on waxed paper, and set it on the picnic table in a patch of shade, and the four of them stood around it like people around a fire, waiting to see if it would set.

While they waited, Kylee went to the car for her sunglasses, and she came back holding the bag of chocolate she'd left on the back seat yesterday, the store-bought bars they'd been saving for s'mores. "These look weird," she said. "Are they ruined?" The bars were streaked with a dull grey film, wispy and white in places, like fog had settled on them and stayed. Jack took one and turned it under the light. The chocolate underneath smelled fine. It was just the surface, and something about it snagged in his mind, a word from one of the videos surfacing slowly.

"Fat bloom," he said. "That's what that's called." He held the bar up so Barrett and Mr. Tremblay could see it. "It's that grey or white streaky film that shows up on chocolate that wasn't tempered right in the first place, or that melted and reset on its own. The car got hot yesterday. It melted and came back, but not the right way." The bar had done, without him, everything he was trying to do with the thermometer and the slab, and it had failed in a way he could now name. There was something almost comforting in that. Failure had a shape. It was legible.

The spoon set in eleven minutes. Jack broke off the edge and it snapped, cleanly, with a sound like a small dry branch, and the shine held even when he tilted it into the direct sun. Kylee ate the fat-bloomed bar anyway and shrugged, because it tasted the same, which Jack filed away as another fact that didn't fit neatly anywhere. He laid out the next batch of molds, checked the stove's flame, and glanced at Mr. Tremblay, who raised his coffee mug a half inch, as if adjourning the session until further evidence. "Same numbers again?" Barrett asked. "Or are you changing something?" Jack looked at the thermometer, then at the streaked bar still lying open on the table between them. "Same numbers," he said. "But this time I'm writing down everything."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: A useful way to predict temperature effects is to treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction and as a reactant of an endothermic one.
story:
The chemistry exhibit on the third floor had a copper chloride solution in a sealed flask, plumbed to a coil that ran through hot water on one side and ice water on the other. Violet had walked past it twice already, following Rebecca, who was mapping the whole museum on her phone because she wanted to see the planetarium show at two and the robotics lab at three and somehow both. Finley trailed behind them both with a worksheet from Ms. Joseph, half filled out, the pen capped.

"Equilibrium shift," Violet read off the placard. "When temperature changes, the balance changes." The flask at the cold end had gone a deep blue, and near the heat, faint and washed toward green, like something deciding.

Rebecca tugged her sleeve. "Twenty minutes, then planetarium. You can stare at juice later."

"Chill," said Finley, and then looked annoyed at himself.

Ms. Joseph's worksheet had one question they couldn't answer, the one that had sat blank on Violet's desk for a week: which way does the reaction shift when you heat it? Violet had memorized the rule about concentration, the one about pressure, but temperature refused to sit still in her head. Every time she thought she had it, it turned over. She'd had a presentiment all week, sitting in the back of class, that the exam would land exactly on the thing she couldn't hold.

The demo had a lever. HOT on one side, COLD on the other, and a neutral middle. Violet pulled the lever to HOT and watched the coil flush the flask. The green spread. The blue retreated. Then she reversed it, and the color crept back the other way, slow, patient, like it had all the time in the world.

"Write down what you see," Finley said, uncapping his pen at last. "Heated: shifts toward green. Cooled: shifts toward blue." He copied the chart from the placard, which listed the two reaction directions with stubborn blandness and no arrows, no hint of which way anything went or why.

"That's the observation, not the rule," Violet said. "Ms. Joseph wants us to predict, not just watch."

"So interpolate," Rebecca said, not looking up from her phone. "You've got hot and you've got cold. What's between them?"

"That's not the problem. I can interpolate. The problem is I don't know why heating pushes it that way, so on the exam, with a different reaction, I'll guess." Violet pulled the lever back and forth, watching the colors argue. The placard said exothermic. She said the word out loud, trying it. "This direction is exothermic. So it gives off heat."

"Then heating it should make it not want to give off more," Finley said.

"That's a feeling, not a reason." But she was already digging in her bag for the worksheet, and she turned it over and wrote the equation on the blank back, two species with a double arrow between them. She stared at it. Then, on the right side, after the products, she added one more thing in parentheses: heat. On the left, nothing.

Rebecca glanced over. "You can't just write heat into the equation."

"Watch me," Violet said, but she said it slowly, because something was settling. If heat sat on the product side, then the whole concentration rule she already trusted would work on it like anything else. Heating the flask meant adding more of a product, and adding a product pushed the reaction backward, away from green, toward blue. But the flask had gone green when heated. So the equation as she'd written it was wrong. She erased the parentheses from the right side and wrote them on the left instead, before the reactants. Heat as a reactant. Then heating it meant adding a reactant, and the system would push forward, to green, to get rid of what she'd added. That matched the flask. That matched the color she'd watched crawl through the coil.

"So this one's endothermic in the forward direction," she said. "It takes heat in. That's why the green wins when it's hot." And then, testing it against the rule she was borrowing: if it were exothermic instead, heat would sit on the product side like she'd first written, and cooling it would pull the reaction forward. She checked that against the placard's other reaction, the one that turned cloudy when the coil ran through ice. It fit. Both directions, both reactions, one idea doing all the work.

Finley copied her equation, parentheses and all. "This better be right," he said. "Ms. Joseph is going to ask."

"It fits everything here. Whether it fits everything everywhere," Violet said, "I don't know yet."

The planetarium announcement chimed overhead. Rebecca closed her map app with a violence that suggested she'd been waiting for the sound all day. "Now. Both of you. You can bring the paper, you can't bring the flask."

Violet took one last look at the coil, blue at the ice end, green at the hot, both colors holding steady at their own temperatures. Then she folded the worksheet along the crease she'd made and followed them toward the stairs.

"Hey," Finley said, catching up. "If she asks us where we learned it, are we telling her a juice display?"

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A join with no matching condition returns every combination of rows, so 100 customers and 1,000 orders produce 100,000 rows.
story:
Youcef's basement smelled of cardamom tea and old carpet, and the laptop on the folding table had a fan that whined like a trapped insect. Chase pulled his chair in and typed the join he had been sketching in his notebook all week, the one that was supposed to answer Mr. Sandhu's challenge question: which customers had never ordered anything. He hit Enter.

The screen froze. Not instantly, the way a crash feels, but slowly, the progress bar at the bottom of the window creeping like something wading through syrup. Rows began to appear, faster and faster, scrolling into a blur of names and numbers that had no business being next to each other. Mrs. Adeyemi from Leeds paired with an order for forty kilograms of fencing wire. A customer from Osaka matched to somebody's grocery run. The row counter climbed past ten thousand and kept going.

"What did you do," Youcef said. It was not a question. He leaned over Chase's shoulder, and Janessa, sprawled on the couch with her calculus homework, put her phone down.

"I joined them. Customers to orders. Like the notes said."

"Your notes have an ON clause," Janessa said. She came over anyway, because Janessa always came over, even when she had already decided whose fault it was.

Chase scrolled up through his query. He had written JOIN orders and then, in his hurry, gone straight to SELECT. Without the condition matching customer to order, the database had simply paired everything with everything. He did the arithmetic in the margin of his notebook: the practice database had one hundred customers and one thousand orders, and the counter on screen was still climbing toward a hundred thousand rows. Every combination of rows. The fan whined louder, and Youcef reached past him and pulled the plug.

In the sudden quiet, the house above them was crepuscular with late afternoon, the small window at ground level letting in one slanted bar of light that caught the dust. Chase sat with his hands flat on the table.

"It's not broken," Youcef said. "It's just thinking very hard about a very stupid question."

"That's not a stupid question, that's the question," Chase said. "Mr. Sandhu wants the customers who ordered nothing. That's the whole assignment." He turned in his chair. "But they're not in the orders table at all. How do I find something by its absence?"

Janessa picked up his notebook and read his sketch. She was the one who had told him last week, in the hallway, that coding was for people who liked being wrong in public, and he had not spoken to her for two days over it. Since then they had arrived at a wary rapprochement, mostly by way of her handing him half a sandwich and him not saying anything about the half she kept. She tapped his diagram of the two tables with her pen.

"You're drawing it like they overlap," she said. "But the people you want are outside the overlap. Draw the whole customer circle, and the part of it with no order attached."

He drew it. One hundred customers, whole, and the orders reaching into it from the side, and a crescent of customers no order touched. The word LEFT surfaced in his memory from somewhere in the notes, left join, and he understood it suddenly as a direction of loyalty: keep the left table entire, and where the right one had nothing to offer, put emptiness in. NULL. He did not say the word out loud yet because he was not sure, and he had learned tonight what certainty cost.

He waited for the laptop to come back to life, rewrote the query with LEFT JOIN and the ON condition matching customer numbers, and added a WHERE that asked for the emptiness: where the order column is null. The fan gave one ordinary hum. Eleven rows came back. Eleven customers, out of one hundred, who had never ordered a thing, their names sitting quietly in the result like stones at low tide.

"That's them," Youcef said. "That's actually them."

"Maybe," Chase said. He was looking at one name, a customer from March, with no orders and no note explaining why. "Or eleven broken records, or eleven refunds nobody logged. The query finds the absence. It doesn't tell you why the absence is there." He copied the eleven names into his notebook, circumscribing each one in a loose loop of ink, though he did not know yet what he would do with them.

Janessa had gone back to the couch, but she was watching him over her calculus book. "So what's your answer for Sandhu?"

"The answer is the query, and the eleven names, and a paragraph saying which part I'm still guessing at." He closed the notebook. Then, because the light was almost gone and the fan had gone quiet and it seemed possible now, he said, "You want to stay for the eleven names? I'll read them out."

She put down the book. "Read me the March one first."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Elliot was not nervous, which was obvious from the way he sat perfectly still with his hands folded, except that his right knee was going like a sewing machine and he had read the poster about tetanus boosters four times without absorbing a single word.

He was here for a test. That was the whole errand, uncomplicated, a thing an adult does: you call the clinic, you say you'd like to be tested for infections, you give a name, you show up. The receptionist had not batted an eye, which Elliot found both reassuring and slightly deflating, as though he had rehearsed a difficult speech and been handed a coupon.

The complication was Beatrice, who had agreed to come with him and then, in the parking lot, had confessed the actual reason she'd come. Her cousin, sixteen, had asked her questions she couldn't answer, and Beatrice had said, immediately and without consulting him, "Ask Elliot, he knows all of it," and now here she was with a list on her phone, and here was Elliot, who was absolutely the right person for this, as he was calm, informed, and unembarrassable, a reputation he had built primarily through one class presentation and a great deal of luck.

He had not felt lucky at the time. The presentation had been assigned by Ms. Andersen in the spring, contraception and consent, the kind of topic where the room goes quiet in a bad way. Elliot had prepared by reading everything, including a page Lionel had found and read aloud with the flat incredulity of a boy reading a customs form. "With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy," Lionel had announced, "mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time." He'd looked up. "Thirteen? The box makes it sound bulletproof."

Elliot remembered standing at the front with his note cards, hearing that number land somewhere in his own chest. He had planned a tidy presentation, cause and effect, points one through five, and instead he'd heard himself say that the box wasn't lying exactly, it just wasn't telling the whole truth, that the number on the box was the method working perfectly and the number in real life was people being people, tired people, hurried people, people who'd had two beers and skipped the part where you pinch the tip. He'd said, "The gap between those two numbers is basically the whole conversation," and Ms. Andersen had written something down, and he had chosen to believe it was a compliment.

"It's mostly about the gap," he told Beatrice now, quietly, because she had started asking while they waited. "The pill pack says one thing, the real world says another, and you have to tell people both numbers or you're lying to them in a friendly way." Beatrice asked what you do about it, and he said you explain typical use, you explain that using something correctly every single time is harder than it sounds, you explain that combining methods is how you close the gap, and you do it without making anyone feel stupid, because the moment someone feels stupid they stop listening.

"The consent part," Beatrice said, scrolling her list. "He asked how you even know if it's yes."

"That one's simpler and harder," Elliot said. "Yes has to be awake, sober, enthusiastic, and it can be taken back at any point, including the middle. If you have to talk someone into it, it's not yes, it's a negotiation you rigged." He was pleased with that line, so pleased that he heard himself delivering a version of it to a room of imagined freshmen, voluble and gracious, fielding questions. Beatrice wrote it down word for word, which moderated his enthusiasm somewhat, since written down it looked less like wisdom and more like something a person says in a clinic waiting room.

"You've done this before?" she asked.

"Once," he said, which was true, and also the most misleading thing he'd said all morning. He had done it once, badly, at a party in June, the dialectic of his own head going full tilt: the version of him who knew everything versus the version of him standing in a hallway with a girl who'd gone quiet. The knowing version had won, eventually, by which he meant he'd said "we don't have to" and she'd exhaled like he'd removed something heavy from her arms, and they'd gone back to the kitchen and eaten chips, and he had spent the whole drive home alternating between feeling heroic and suspecting that feeling heroic about the bare minimum was its own kind of vanity. He did not mention any of this to Beatrice. He only said, "Once," and let his face suggest experience.

"Elliot?" The nurse at the door had a clipboard and the unremarkable efficiency of someone who says forty names a day. He stood, and his knees did the thing where they report to his brain a half second late, and Beatrice said, "Wait, so what do I tell him about the testing part? Where does his cousin even go?"

"You go anywhere like this," Elliot said, standing halfway between her and the nurse, aware that he was blocking the doorway and that the nurse was waiting. "You call, you say you want testing, they ask a couple of questions, it's mostly a urine sample or a swab, some of it's a blood draw, and results come back in a few days by whatever method you pick. Nobody yells at you. Nobody tells your parents if you don't want them to. You can bring someone." He was aware that he was talking fast, that the nurse could hear all of it, that his ears were doing something warm. "Tell him it takes twenty minutes and it's the most boring brave thing you'll ever do."

The nurse, unmoved by his entire existence, said, "This way," and Elliot followed her down the hallway, past a poster about flu season, rehearsing the answers to questions no one had asked him yet.

"Text me the boring brave thing," Beatrice called after him. "I'm putting it in the list."

"It's copyrighted," he called back, and the exam room door swung shut behind him on its slow hinge, and he sat down on the crinkling paper and, being not nervous at all, checked the tetanus poster for a fifth time, but they hadn't put one in here, so he read the reminder about hand washing on the back of the door instead, twice, all the way through.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Percent yield is the actual mass of product obtained divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and copper sulfate, and Carter had cleared the workbench down to a single square of white paper on which his crystals sat like blue glass. He had grown them for the science fair over six weeks, and last night, when he finally weighed them, the scale had read 11.2 grams. His notebook said there should have been 14.0. He had checked the arithmetic three times before bed and twice this morning, and the numbers refused to change, so the problem was somewhere else, somewhere in the chemistry, and he had until Thursday to find it.

Johnathan arrived on his bike with his backpack still on, because he had come straight from summer practice. "You said it was urgent," he said, dropping the bag by the lawnmower.

"It's the yield." Carter turned the notebook so Johnathan could see the page. "I started with the copper sulfate, I did the whole thing, molar mass and everything, grams to moles, moles to grams of product. Fourteen grams theoretical. Eleven point two actual. That's a real difference, not a rounding thing."

Johnathan leaned on the bench and looked at the crystals the way he looked at a defense he hadn't scouted yet. "So you messed up a step."

"That's what I thought. But look." Carter walked him through it slowly, pointing with a pencil. Twenty-five grams of the pentahydrate, divided by its molar mass of two hundred forty-nine point seven grams per mole, gave him point one zero zero moles. Point one zero zero moles of product, times its molar mass of one hundred forty grams per mole, gave fourteen grams. The conversion from mass to moles and back had a symmetry that used to beguile him, the way the same number of particles could be reached from either side, but this morning the symmetry felt like a trap, because it had promised him fourteen grams and delivered eleven point two.

Kellan showed up twenty minutes late with two energy drinks and less patience. He was going into business, not chemistry, and he made a point of saying so. "It's a high school fair," he said, cracking the can. "Nobody's going to re-weigh your rocks."

"The rocks aren't the point," Carter said. "If I can't explain why I got less than I predicted, then I don't actually understand what I did."

From where Johnathan sat on an overturned bucket, watching Carter copy numbers onto a fresh sheet, the whole scene looked different than it had an hour ago. He had come over expecting to babysit a friend through panic, and instead Carter was calm in a way Johnathan recognized from film sessions, the quiet of someone who has decided the problem can be solved and is now only deciding in what order. Johnathan had spent three years treating Carter's science stuff as a private quirk, a parochial interest that didn't overlap with anything Johnathan cared about. Sitting in the garage, he found himself doing the division in his head before Carter could, and liking it.

"Wait," Johnathan said. "You said eleven point two out of fourteen. So what fraction did you actually get?"

"Point eight." Carter wrote it. Then, because the idea had been forming since breakfast and only now had somewhere to land, he said, "There's a thing this is called. Percent yield. Actual mass of product divided by the theoretical yield, times a hundred."

"That's it? That's the whole thing?"

"That's the whole thing." Carter worked it out on the sheet: eleven point two divided by fourteen point zero, times one hundred, equals eighty percent. He looked at the number for a long moment. "Eighty percent yield. Some of my product just isn't there."

Kellan drifted over, drawn in despite himself, and peered at the sheet. "Eighty sounds good though. Eighty on a test is a B-plus."

"Tests don't work like that," Carter said. "A test measures what I know. This measures what happened in the beaker." He was aware, even as he said it, that he had changed his mind about something larger and hadn't fully articulated it yet. For six weeks he had thought the project was the crystals. Now he thought the project was the gap, the missing twenty percent, the honest accounting between what theory promised and what the scale reported. He could present a perfect crystal and a perfect calculation, and the interesting thing was that they disagreed.

Mr. Gagnon from next door came through the side door without knocking, the way he did, holding a jar of washers he had apparently come to borrow the drill for. He saw the setup, the scale, the blue crystals, and the sheet of arithmetic, and asked only one question, which was whether the scale was level. Carter checked it. It was. Mr. Gagnon nodded, took the drill, and left, and somehow the brief visit settled the matter more than an hour of explanation would have, because it meant the equipment was fine and the discrepancy was real.

"So Thursday," Johnathan said, gathering his bag as the light went orange through the garage door's little window. "What do you actually tell them?"

Carter picked up the crystal with the tweezers and held it against the last of the sun. "I tell them I predicted fourteen grams and I got eighty percent of that, and that I don't fully know where the rest went yet."

Kellan raised his can half an inch, like a toast. "Eighty's still a B-plus."

"Then I'm going to find my twenty percent," Carter said, and set the crystal back on the white paper, blue and sharp and exactly as heavy as it was.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Cutting an onion breaks its cells and releases enzymes that produce syn-propanethial-S-oxide, a vapor that irritates the eyes and makes them tear.
story:
Nicole held the onion at arm's length like it had insulted her, which, in a way, it had. The community kitchen on Marsh Street ran four industrial burners and a soup pot the size of a bathtub, and tonight it was hers to command, because her mother had pulled a double shift and the family's dinner had landed, by text message and mild guilt, on Nicole. Soup, the text said. Something with vegetables. Your brother will eat it if you don't tell him what's in it.

She set the onion on the cutting board and started to dice, and within four strokes her eyes were flooding. Her brother, perched on a counter stool supposedly doing homework, pointed at her face and grinned. "You're crying over soup. That's the saddest thing I've ever seen."

"I'm not crying. It's chemistry." She wiped her cheek with her sleeve, which only relocated the sting. "Cutting the onion breaks its cells and lets out enzymes that make this vapor, syn-propanethial-S-oxide, and it gets in your eyes and makes them water. It's not sadness, it's physiology." Saying the word out loud helped, the way naming a monster sometimes does.

Lennon, who had drifted in from the pantry with a jar of paprika and no explanation, considered this. "So the onion is attacking you."

"The onion is defending itself."

"Seems inefficient. Crying never stopped me from eating anything."

Soleil arrived ten minutes later, hair still wet from swim practice, and took over the stirring while Nicole rebuilt her composure at the sink. Ms. Santos, who ran the kitchen and had a talent for appearing exactly when someone misused her equipment, watched Nicole pick up the knife again and offered one sentence before vanishing toward the walk-in cooler: "Sharp knife, fewer crushed cells." Nicole filed that away. It sounded true, and later, when she tested it against a second onion with the whetted blade, it mostly was.

The problem, the actual one, arrived with the tasting. Nicole had planned a straightforward soup, her mother's method, everything boiled together until the vegetables surrendered. But Soleil kept arguing for roasting the carrots and peppers first, the way her grandmother did, because roasting caramelized the sugars and made everything deeper. And Lennon, who had appointed himself quality control, kept sneaking spoonfuls and offering notes with the gravity of a judge on a cooking show. "It's fine," he said, in the tone of someone who means it is not fine. "It's warm water with ambition."

"Be facetious somewhere else," Nicole said, though she had to admit, privately, that the broth was thin, that her mother's version had a richness this one lacked. Her instinct was loyalty: do it the way it had always been done, because that was the taste of home, because the recipe was a kind of inheritance. Soleil's instinct was improvement: a soup should be as good as it could be, regardless of whose kitchen it came from. For a while Nicole stood between the two positions, wooden spoon in hand, feeling the actual weight of a decision that was, objectively, about carrots.

She decided to do both. She roasted the carrots and one onion until their edges blackened sweetly, then added them to the pot her mother would have recognized, with the barley and the bay leaf and the pinch of sugar that had always seemed strange until tonight, when Nicole understood it as a small bribe to the tomatoes. Was it her mother's soup or Soleil's grandmother's? Honestly, she couldn't say, and she suspected the answer would keep shifting depending on who was eating it and how homesick they were. What she knew was that the broth had gone amber and thick, that Lennon had stopped narrating and started just eating, and that some hybrid thing, part inheritance and part invention, was simmering in front of her.

Her brother, who had teased her about crying, ate two bowls and asked what was different. "Science," Nicole said, and left it there. She packed the leftovers into containers, one for her mother at the hospital, one for Ms. Santos, who had earned it with the knife advice, and one for the walk home tomorrow when the soup would be even better. Soleil dried the last pot while Lennon put chairs on tables, and Nicole looked at the cutting board where two onion halves sat, innocent as anything, little biochemical fortresses that had lost the battle and won the war. She slid them into the compost and rinsed the board.

"You could wear goggles next time," Lennon said from the doorway.

"I'm not wearing goggles."

"Swim goggles. Soleil has like four pairs."

Soleil threw a dish towel at his head, and Nicole laughed until she had to hold the counter.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: Melodies are often built from four-bar phrases, so a sixteen-bar melody commonly falls into four phrases.
story:
Ms. Mendoza had given them until Friday, and it was already Wednesday lunch, which meant Alexis was eating her sandwich in the music room with manuscript paper instead of a napkin, because she had used the napkin to blot a chord she now regretted.

"Sixteen bars," Tyrell said, leaning over her shoulder. "You've got, what, five?"

"Six and a half. And the half is a lie." She pointed at bar seven, which contained one note and a lot of hope. "Every time I try to write the whole thing at once, it turns into a snake that eats its own tail."

Bella slid into the chair opposite, opened her chips with the ceremony of someone who believed snacking was a competitive sport. "Mine's grandiose. Ms. Mendoza's word. She wrote it in the margin. I think she meant it as a diagnosis."

"Mine's not grandiose. Mine's just long and lost." Alexis spun her pencil. "I keep thinking I have to know where the whole thing ends before I can start, like it's an affidavit I have to swear to in advance."

Tyrell frowned at the page. "Okay, but you play piano, right? Like, actual songs?"

"Badly."

"Badly is a spectrum. Play the first bit." He nudged the keyboard bench with his foot until she gave in and played her six and a half bars, the half bar trailing off into an apologetic silence.

"Okay," Bella said through chips. "The first four bars sound like a thing. The next two and a half sound like a different thing that got mugged."

Alexis looked at the paper. She had been thinking of the melody as one long sentence she had to finish in a single breath, but the first four bars did hold together, and what fell apart was the join. She drew a vertical line after bar four, then, feeling reckless, another after bar eight, and another after twelve, and one more at sixteen, so the empty staff was suddenly four small rooms instead of one enormous hallway.

"Wait," Tyrell said. "That's not cheating?"

"Is it cheating to cut a sandwich into quarters?" Bella said. "Because I do that and nobody arrests me."

"Ms. Mendoza never said it was cheating," Alexis said slowly. "She said 'four phrases.' I wrote it down and then ignored it because I thought she was being poetic." She wasn't sure, though. Four bars to a phrase, four phrases to a melody. It fit what she'd played, but she'd played only one phrase and half a corpse, so the evidence was thin. Maybe some melodies breathed differently. Maybe hers would want to.

Tyrell had been shaking his head, but he stopped. "Actually, you know what, that's how I memorize rap verses. Four bars, four bars, on and on. It's not cheating, it's how anybody fits anything in their head." He grabbed a scrap of manuscript and drew his own four boxes. "Hand me the pencil, I'm going to try something."

While he scribbled, Alexis filled her second phrase, and this time it moved, because she wasn't carrying the whole sixteen bars in her arms at once, only four. She titrated the chord change carefully, half a step of motion where she'd been pouring a whole octave over everything like syrup. Bar nine to twelve came out almost tender, which surprised her, and she played it twice to make sure it wasn't an accident.

"It's not an accident," Bella said. "It's the second-best thing you've played today."

"What's first?"

"Bar five. The mugged one. Keep the mugging, it's got personality."

By the time the bell rang for fifth period, Alexis had thirteen bars, one of them stolen back from the napkin blot, and a hole where phrase four should begin. Tyrell had four bars of something he refused to play in public. Bella had added a key change to hers and then, reading Ms. Mendoza's margin note again, taken it back out, muttering that grandiosity was a slippery slope and she had a reputation to think of, which was funny because she did not.

Thursday night Alexis sat at the kitchen table past eleven, playing the melody in her head because her mother was asleep. She still didn't know whether the four-phrase shape was a law or just a habit that lots of good songs kept, and she wrote both possibilities in the margin like a person hedging a bet. Then she wrote the last phrase anyway: a quiet answer that ended a step lower than the first phrase had begun, the way a question sounds when you've stopped needing it answered.

Friday morning, she handed the pages in, and Tyrell leaned across the aisle and whispered, "If mine gets called grandiose, I'm transferring schools."

Ms. Mendoza read Alexis's melody straight through at the piano, all sixteen bars, and at the end she looked up and said, "Phrase four is my favorite."

"Mine too," Alexis said, and it was even true.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: In a LEFT JOIN, putting a condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, like orders.total > 0, removes the NULL rows and makes it act like an inner join.
story:
Rebecca had agreed to teach herself SQL over the summer because the internship paid nineteen dollars an hour and because Devin had a kitchen table, air conditioning, and a laptop with a working fan. She arrived at his house at ten in the morning with a notebook, two granola bars, and the specific dread of a person about to learn something she could not yet picture. The table smelled like coffee and the ghost of toast. Devin slid over to make room without waking his screen fully.

The exercise came from a free course. Two tables, customers and orders, and a task that sounded like a riddle: find the customers who had never ordered anything. "It's a left join," Rebecca said. "Customers on the left, orders on the right. The ones with no order show up with blanks." She typed it, ran it, and there they were, a tidy list of twelve names with NULL marching down the order columns like a diagnosis. She felt something in her chest unclench. This was learnable. She could learn this.

Devin's mother came through in scrubs on her way to a shift, gathering keys, a laminated badge, a thermos. She worked at a law office downtown, and that morning she was fretting aloud about a subpoena that had arrived misaddressed, which meant, she said, someone else's case file was sitting in their mailroom like a live grenade. She kissed Devin's head, told Rebecca there were string cheese sticks in the fridge drawer, and left. The door's closing changed the pressure in the room slightly. Rebecca saved her file.

Then she ruined it. The task had a second part: total value greater than zero, orders only above a certain amount, and she added a line to the WHERE clause. When she ran the query again, her twelve customers had become eight hundred and forty, all of them people with orders. She sat back. "That's not the same question," she said. Devin leaned over, chewing a string cheese stick he had retrieved without ceremony. "You asked for people with no orders," he said, "and got people with many orders. Impressive, honestly."

Rebecca remembered then, a flashback arriving with the smell of the coffee, of Braedon at the spring job fair explaining why he'd dropped the same course. He'd said the tables turned on you the moment you thought you'd won, that the language smiled and then took your lunch money. She had thought he was being dramatic. Braedon once cried during a dodgeball unit and then claimed it was pollen, so his testimony had a credibility problem, but sitting at Devin's table she conceded the point silently, on his behalf, retroactively.

She tried the filter in the join condition instead of the WHERE clause, because the course notes had a diagram with a shaded overlap and a sentence about where conditions belonged, and the diagram had seemed decorative at the time. Twelve names returned. She moved the condition back to WHERE. Eight hundred and forty. Back to the join: twelve. She did this twice more, slowly, like a person checking a sore tooth. "The WHERE clause is filtering out the NULL rows," she said. "A condition on the right table in the WHERE clause, like orders.total greater than zero, removes the NULLs, and the whole thing acts like an inner join."
